metadata.title: TheLostParticles_TiantongZhang
metadata.audience: Course reviewers reading a Godot particle-effect pass
metadata.greeting_note: hello lexicon: Sawubona (Zulu), one word. Wagwan is Bear's alone.

beats.role_note: WALKER BOOKEND 1/4 - ClaudeComposerAsk. The prompt is a reconstruction and is said aloud to be one. Liam is named in the first breath.
beats.narration_text: Sawubona - this is Liam, in for Bear. The prompt on screen is a reconstruction, written to be illustrative. It was never sent. The game under it is real: a dungeon slice in Godot four, three spike traps and a character who can walk and jump. What we are taking apart is three particle effects, and the one question that decides whether any of this is evidence - what can a run that draws nothing actually tell you.

props.command: Please use Walker to add particle effects to my game design document about The Lost - a side-view dungeon crawler where every hazard announces itself before it can hurt you. The spike trap needs grit when it strikes and the room needs air. Write the scenes and the tests; the verdict on how they look in play is mine.
props.runningText: RECONSTRUCTION - this prompt was never sent

beats.role_note: WALKER BOOKEND 2/4 - hesitant writer, one working single-word correction with measured time to complete it.
beats.narration_text: Here is what actually changed. Three particle effects, six emitters between them. A grit burst that fires - correction - that spawns a fresh instance every time a trap strikes. A field of motes that is already full on the first frame the room is drawn. And dust under the feet, on an event this game does not have. Two hundred and forty nine automated checks stand behind that, twenty six of them run three times over at three different frame rates, and two deliberate breakages stand behind the checks.

props.text:
Three effects. Six emitters.
A burst that fires per event.
249 checks, 301 results.
One tuning revision, kept.

contextItems.label: By hand
contextItems.detail: The brief, every verdict, the shader conversion.

contextItems.label: Predicted first
contextItems.detail: 7 failures named in the brief. 2 were run.

beats.role_note: C1 CODE. The event already existed. Paired with B03.
beats.narration_text: Every effect needs an event, and this one was already here. The trap is a five-state machine, and the frame it enters FIRING it emits a signal called fired. That line was written for Assignment Five and nothing in this assignment touched it. The spawner connects to it, binds the trap that sent it so it knows where to put the burst, and instances a fresh scene. Note what it does not do. It does not reuse one node and set emitting to true, because on a one-shot emitter that is already emitting, that call does nothing at all - the second of two close events is silently dropped. And it parents the burst to the room, not to the trap, so nothing can free it mid-life.

props.title: The event, and why it is a signal
props.code:
State.FIRING:
			warn_amount = 1.0
			_sprite.texture = TEX_FIRED
			fired.emit()
			for body in _hurt_area.get_overlapping_bodies():
				if body.has_method("take_damage"):
					body.take_damage(1)
					player_hit.emit()

notes.label: Why not a new signal
notes.value: fired already existed at line 24. Presentation reads game state; it never adds to it.

notes.label: Why an instance per event
notes.value: emitting = true on a busy one_shot node does not restart it. Two close events, one burst.

cues.label: the signal the burst listens for
and the damage, on the same frame

beats.role_note: C1 RESULT. take-p, PLAYED: held keys through the real input map, nothing teleported. The take asserts three traps fired, four bursts and twenty five step-dust puffs before a frame of it counts.
beats.narration_text: There it is, on the game's own event. The trap goes red, the spikes arrive, and the grit comes off the floor line with them. Three traps, three bursts, one walk.

show.event: the first trap begins its warning

beats.role_note: SCRIPTED, not played. take-r emits `fired` at the spawner directly on a 0.20 s rotation. Revision 6.0.2 measured that the ceiling is unreachable in play: traps are 1.17 s apart at 96 px/s and a burst lives 0.60 s.
beats.narration_text: Rapid repeats - and this is not gameplay. The signal is being emitted straight at the spawner, every two tenths of a second. Three alive at once is the ceiling the brief set its budget against, and playing this room reaches one: the traps are one point one seven seconds apart and a burst lives six tenths.

show.event: SCRIPTED label holds through the beat

beats.role_note: C2 CODE. The three parts of a particle system, on one node. Paired with B05.
beats.narration_text: A particle system is three steps and this one node shows all three. Emission is when and how many: amount four, lifetime twelve hundredths of a second, one shot true, explosiveness one, so all four leave together. Process is how they move, and it is not here - it is behind process underscore material, a separate resource with velocity, spread, gravity, damping and the curves. Draw is what reaches the screen: the material property, which carries the additive blend, local coords off so a particle stays where it was born, and visibility rect, which decides when the whole node is culled and never clips a particle. Three names, three steps, and the file keeps them apart.

props.title: Emission, process and draw - on one node
props.code:
[node name="Flash" type="GPUParticles2D" parent="."]
material = SubResource("CIM_add")
emitting = false
amount = 4
process_material = SubResource("PPM_flash")
lifetime = 0.12
one_shot = true
preprocess = 0.0
explosiveness = 1.0
local_coords = false
visibility_rect = Rect2(-48, -64, 96, 96)

notes.label: Emission vs draw
notes.value: amount, lifetime, one_shot, explosiveness: emission. material, visibility_rect: draw.

notes.label: The process half
notes.value: PPM_flash holds velocity, spread, gravity, damping and the curves.

cues.label: process: the whole second step, by reference
draw: culls the node, never clips a particle

beats.role_note: Effect A's tuning revision 6.0.1, with the author's verdict. Fixture capture from godot/previews/hit_burst_preview.tscn, labelled. The per-frame difference counts are recomputed from the committed frames at build time by scripts/compose_particles_evidence.py.
beats.narration_text: This is the tuning loop, and it is the part of the assignment that cannot be automated. Flash was given the job of owning frame one, and at a scale of one point six it came out the same size as the grit beside it. One setting moved - scale min and max, five and seven. Before the recapture, Claude predicted frames ten and twelve would change and the rest would be identical. Five of six landed. Frame twelve is where it was wrong, and not by a little: the two frames are bit-identical, zero pixels different. Flash is drawn additively, so if it contributed any light at all, tripling its base scale would have moved at least one pixel. It contributes nothing by then. The whole visible difference lives on one frame. The verdict in the running game was the author's, and it was keep.

shot.title: One setting, one frame, and the prediction that missed
shot.image_label: r0 left, r1 right, frame 10; the table is recomputed from the frames

show.event: the frame 12 row is marked - zero

beats.role_note: C3 CODE. Effect B, and the feature Effect A does not use. Paired with B07.
beats.narration_text: Effect B is ambience: one emitter, sixty motes, an eight second life, and no event at all. Its condition is the scene being loaded with the player alive, and it stops on the player's died signal. The feature Effect A does not use is on line fifty two. Preprocess, eight point zero - one whole lifetime. The engine simulates the entire field before the first frame is drawn, so the room is never seen filling up. Without it, every single scene load starts in an empty room that fills over eight seconds, and nothing errors, and no headless test in this repository can see it. That is the failure the brief named F4, and the only instrument that catches it is a picture.

props.title: preprocess - the feature Effect A does not use
props.code:
[node name="DungeonMotes" type="GPUParticles2D"]
script = ExtResource("0_condition")
emitting = true
amount = 60
process_material = SubResource("PPM_motes")
lifetime = 8.0
one_shot = false
preprocess = 8.0
explosiveness = 0.0
local_coords = false
visibility_rect = Rect2(0, 0, 640, 200)

notes.label: Why one emitter
notes.value: The effect has one job. A second would be a second job nobody asked for.

notes.label: What stops it
notes.value: player.gd's died signal. emitting goes false; motes already born finish their 8 s.

cues.label: one full lifetime, simulated before frame one

beats.role_note: F4 demonstrated by mutation: the same preview with preprocess set to 0.0 in the scene file and reverted immediately after. Both are FIXTURE captures. Mote pixels are recomputed at build time from the committed frames against frame 340 of the shipped run, which is the same field eight seconds after it stopped - an empty room.
beats.narration_text: Both of these are frame one. Same scene, same preview, one number different. On the left, preprocess at eight: the field is at full density on the first frame anyone could see, and it stays flat. On the right, preprocess at zero: twelve pixels, which is two per cent of the other, climbing to ninety nine by frame forty - about a fifth of the way through a fill that takes eight seconds. Nothing errored. The configuration test passed on both. This difference is only visible to a capture, and that is exactly why the brief put it in the frame strip column and not in a test.

shot.title: The same effect, one number apart, on frame one
shot.path: captures/dungeon_motes/ - FIXTURE, preview scene, mutation reverted
shot.image_label: preprocess 8.0 left, 0.0 right; the table is recomputed from the frames

beats.role_note: take-c, PLAYED: the field running, then the tree paused, then the player killed by walking onto a trap five times. The take asserts the player did not move for 78 paused frames and that emitting went false.
beats.narration_text: The field is running. Now the tree is paused - and the motes freeze with it, because the node inherits its process mode. A paused game with drifting dust reads as a bug.

beats.role_note: take-c, second window: the fifth hit and the eight seconds after it. The tail is 8.6 s because that is one mote lifetime; a three second tail showed a field that looked unchanged, which is true and useless.
beats.narration_text: And this is how it stops. The fifth hit kills the player, emitting goes false - and nothing is cut off. The sixty motes already in the air finish their eight seconds on the colour ramp.

beats.role_note: C4 CODE. The generated process shader. The author converted PPM_dust to a ShaderMaterial in the editor and saved it; the file is a copy, read-only, and nothing in the game loads it. Paired with B09.
beats.narration_text: This is Godot's own process shader, generated by converting the dust emitter's material in the editor. Three hundred and eighty four lines; these two are the ones to read. Line one sixty one multiplies the particle's scale by a texture lookup into scale curve, at the particle's own normalised lifetime. Line one sixty two does the same to its colour through colour ramp. That is what a curve in the Inspector actually is - a one dimensional texture, sampled once per particle per frame, on the graphics card. And look at line one sixty: compile-time add textures. Those two lines only exist because this material carries a ramp and a curve. Convert an empty material and the comment is there with nothing under it.

props.title: Two lines, and what a curve really is

notes.label: Dust 2.0 to 3.5
notes.value: scale_min/max are one mix() at line 150. Line 161 is the curve over life.

notes.label: Why Dust
notes.value: Flash carries both too but lives 0.12 s. Dust grows over 0.45 s, so a strip reads it.

beats.role_note: The two shader lines beside the brief settings they implement, with the engine output those settings produce. Frames 15 and 20 of the kept r1 capture - FIXTURE - where Dust is the only emitter still alive. The deltas are recomputed at build time.
beats.narration_text: And here is what those two lines do to a picture. Frame fifteen and frame twenty of the kept capture, cropped to the trap. Section one point three of the brief gives Dust a scale curve that rises from nought point six to one point eight, and a colour ramp that ends at nothing. Line one sixty one is the first of those and line one sixty two is the second, and between frame ten and frame twenty the burst goes from ten by twelve logical pixels to sixty nine by sixty nine while its brightest channel falls from two hundred and thirty to ninety two. Wider, and dimmer. The settings are rows in a table in a document. The lines are the arithmetic.

shot.title: The brief's rows, the shader's lines, and the frames they make
shot.image_label: frames 15 and 20, cropped to the trap

show.event: the setting and the line pair up

beats.role_note: C5 CODE. Effect C's event does not exist in the game; it is derived from measured position delta. Paired with B11.
beats.narration_text: Effect C is dust under the feet, and this game has no footstep signal. The player script has a position, a velocity and a floor check, and nothing that says a foot just landed. So the event is derived, and the four lines on screen are the whole derivation. Distance travelled on the ground accumulates; every twenty four pixels, one puff. Not a timer, which is right at exactly one speed, and not a per-frame chance, which changes with the frame rate. Two details earn their place. It is a while, not an if, because at thirty frames a second one frame can cover more than one stride. And the spawn is stepped back by the remainder, so the puff lands where the stride actually finished rather than where the player has already got to. Without that line the spacing was three point two pixels out at thirty frames a second and correct at sixty, which is the one thing this effect exists to not do.

props.title: An event this game does not have

notes.label: Why distance
notes.value: A timer is right at one speed. Distance is right at any speed and rate.

notes.label: The back-date
notes.value: _since_step IS the overshoot after the subtraction. Stepping back lands on the crossing.

cues.label: the spawn, stepped back by the overshoot

beats.role_note: C5 RESULT. take-p again, the feet. Played: held keys only. The run east and the run west are in one unbroken take, so the mirror is visible rather than claimed.
beats.narration_text: Twenty five puffs in that take. The trail runs two or three deep, because a puff outlives a stride - and when the player turns, the dust throws the other way.

show.event: the jump, and the landing puff
the dust throws the other way

beats.role_note: C6 CODE. What a headless run can and cannot price. Paired with B11B.
beats.narration_text: Last pair, and it is about the instrument rather than the effect. All three of these are GPU particle nodes, and a headless run uses a dummy renderer: it draws nothing and it runs no particle process at all, because that process is a shader on the card. So the brief predicted that a headless measurement would read approximately zero for every one of them, and predicted it by construction rather than by hope. What is left to measure is the node's own bookkeeping, and the function under that comment is what counts it: how many scene instances each effect created and freed. That is CPU work a headless run does execute in full.

props.title: What a dummy renderer can still weigh

notes.label: Why instances
notes.value: A one-shot effect spawns and frees a scene per event. That is ordinary CPU work.

notes.label: Why not FPS
notes.value: With vsync on, FPS reads the refresh rate with the effects off and the same with them on.

cues.label: the only thing left to weigh
counted once per instance, not per frame

beats.role_note: The recorded output of scripts/run-test.sh cost_effects.gd 60 300, drawn verbatim at build time from evidence/a6/cost-effects.txt, above a frame of take-r with three bursts alive. The GPU budgets are NOT settled by this script and the card says so.
beats.narration_text: The prediction held: microseconds, against budgets written in milliseconds. But read the table the right way round. The ordering is stable - Effect B, one persistent node that creates nothing, is the smallest in both runs, and A and C, which spawn and free a scene per event, are larger. The microsecond figures themselves are not. Effect B moves by three microseconds between the two runs, and each run's own baseline spread claims half of one. The column that holds still is instances, and that is what a headless run is really weighing: not the particle process, which never ran at all, but the cost of making and freeing a scene. None of this settles a budget. The budgets are GPU time, read in the Visual Profiler on hardware, and the brief puts that row under HUMAN for exactly this reason.

shot.title: The headless price, and the one thing it can weigh
shot.image_label: take-r frame, three bursts alive; the table is the recorded output

show.event: the baseline and its noise floor
B below the floor, A and C above it

beats.role_note: WALKER BOOKEND 3/4 - verdict. Implemented work, limitations and human judgment kept apart. Human/AI split, texture sources, revision shown, one next step.
beats.narration_text: So. Written by hand, by the author: the brief, every verdict in the tuning log, and the material conversion that produced the process shader. Written by Claude: three effect scenes, three preview scenes, the two drivers, two hundred and forty nine checks, the cost script and the capture rigs. Measured, not asserted: the stride cadence is the same distance at thirty, sixty and a hundred and forty four frames a second, deviation zero. Preprocess at eight gives a full field on frame one and at zero gives two per cent of it. Three bursts can be alive at once and playing this room reaches one. Textures: there are none. Not one of the six emitters has a texture assigned - the look is colour ramps, scale curves and a blend mode, so there is nothing to credit and nothing to license. Claude's own work needed catching more than once. Four checks that could not fail shipped green, one of them literally written as x or true. A capture helper threw on every call the moment an instance freed itself. And the first generated shader was converted from an empty material - it loaded, it reported the right mode, it declared thirty eight uniforms, and it had no texture call in it at all. The author found that one by counting lines. Still open, and this is the honest part: the GPU times are not read yet, so every budget in the brief is still a prediction. Effect B's loop produced a verdict of keep with no setting changed, which is not the same as a revision. Both B and C drift dust below the floor line, between eleven and twenty nine per cent of it, and the only instrument that sees it is a difference image. The next step is the Visual Profiler, because it is the only number here that can still fail. Everything you have seen came from one game source revision, named on the card.

props.artifactHeading: Who wrote what, and what was measured
artifactLines: By hand: the brief, every tuning verdict, the material conversion.
By Claude: 3 effect scenes, 3 previews, 2 drivers, 249 checks, the rigs.
Measured: stride cadence identical at 30 / 60 / 144 fps, 0.0000 px deviation.
Measured: preprocess 8.0 gives 518 mote px on frame 1; 0.0 gives 12.
Measured: 3 bursts can overlap; playing this room reaches 1. Peak in play 32.
Textures: none. No emitter has one - ramps, curves and a blend mode only.
Caught in Claude's work: 4 checks that could not fail; a shader from an empty material.
Open: no GPU time yet, so every budget is a prediction. Next: the Visual Profiler.

beats.role_note: WALKER BOOKEND 4/4 - Your Turn. One bounded change with a prediction. Liam signs off here, not on the outro card.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take the prompt on screen, then do the bounded version yourself. Open any particle effect you have and find the one setting whose job you could not demonstrate if someone asked. Write down what the frame should look like with that setting at its default, before you change anything. Then change it, capture the same frame in engine, and count the pixels that moved. If the number is zero, you have just learned that the setting does nothing where you thought it did - and that is a finding, not a mistake. The whole discipline is writing the prediction down first, because a prediction you write afterwards is a description. Liam, signing off.

props.command: Please use Walker to capture the same six frames of my particle effect before and after one setting change, and count the pixels that differ on each frame. I will write the prediction into the brief first. Tell me plainly which frames disagree with what I wrote.
props.runningText: one setting, and a prediction written first
